Definition: Percentage of the national population covered by at least one 4G/LTE mobile network signal, whether or not they subscribe to the service. 4G is the practical minimum for meaningful broadband connectivity enabling digital services.
Comments: ITU report summary states ~75% of population covered by higher-generation networks (3G/4G).
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Confirmed. ITU DataHub data (via the CTO country profile, sourced from Cameroon's telecoms regulator ART) puts population coverage by at least LTE/WiMAX at 70% in 2022, within the 50-74% band, corroborating the original single-source estimate. A 2026 Xalam Analytics data-centre market brief separately claims >90% 4G coverage, but this is a market brief, not a dedicated coverage survey; flagged for human review given the discrepancy, while the regulator-sourced ITU figure is preferred here.

Definition: Whether the country has an operational Internet Exchange Point (IXP) and its maturity. IXPs enable local internet traffic to be exchanged domestically rather than being routed internationally, reducing latency, costs, and dependence on foreign infrastructure. Critical for local digital ecosystem development.
Comments: CAMIX listed in PeeringDB as national IXP with PoPs in Douala and Yaoundé (active).
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Confirmed with a fresher primary source. CAMIX's own member directory lists 14 active peers (Camtel, MTN, Orange, Creolink, Matrix Telecoms, Newtelnet, ST-Digital, plus Akamai as a CDN) across 3 PoPs in Douala and Yaoundé, consistent with 'active IXP(s) with moderate participation'.

Definition: Unique mobile subscriber penetration rate as a percentage of the total population. Measures the proportion of individuals who subscribe to a mobile service (not SIM cards, which can be multiple per person). Mobile phones are the primary device for internet access in Africa.
Comments: GSMA Intelligence (via DataReportal) reports 23.92m mobile connections in early 2023, equivalent to 84.6% of population.
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Revised down. The variable requires unique-subscriber penetration, not SIM/connections penetration, but the cited (and all newly found) figures of 84-96% are GSMA 'connections', which include multi-SIM users. The World Bank's Cameroon Digital Economy Assessment records unique-subscriber penetration at only ~45% in 2017 against ~70% connections penetration that year — a persistent ~25pp multi-SIM gap. Applying that gap to current connections (86-96%, DataReportal 2024-2025) implies unique-subscriber penetration of roughly 55-65%, i.e. band 4, not band 5. Current GSMA Intelligence unique-subscriber data for Cameroon is paywalled; flagged for human review to confirm against a primary GSMA figure.

Definition: Percentage of mobile connections using smartphones (as opposed to feature phones or basic phones). Smartphones are the minimum device requirement for accessing most digital public infrastructure services, apps, and mobile internet.
Comments: Article citing GSMA says 15.18m smartphones in use in 2022; without total connections denominator this supports mid-range smartphone adoption (40–59%).
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Downgraded to Unknown. On reading it, the cited source's 57.7% figure is Cameroon's share of CEMAC-wide smartphone devices (15.18m of 26.3m regional devices), not Cameroon's own smartphone-adoption rate as a share of its mobile connections — the original calculation conflates the two and does not actually support a 40-59% score. No Cameroon-specific smartphone-adoption percentage was found in open sources; GSMA Intelligence's country-level figure is subscription-only, and the 2025 GSMA Africa-wide average (63% of connections) is not a valid country substitute. Flagged for human review to source the GSMA Intelligence Cameroon figure directly.

Definition: Whether the country has enacted legal or regulatory requirements mandating that certain categories of data (personal data, government data, financial data, or critical infrastructure data) be stored within national borders. Central to data sovereignty debates in Africa.
Value Name: Comprehensive requirements for personal data or broad categories
Comments: Law No. 2024/017 requires authorisation for cross-border transfers and registration/authorisation obligations, implying strong localisation/transfer controls.
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Confirmed by reading the primary legal text. Law No. 2024/017 (23 Dec 2024) requires prior authorisation from the new Personal Data Protection Authority (APDP) for any cross-border transfer of personal data and applies broadly across personal data categories, consistent with 'comprehensive requirements for personal data or broad categories'. Enforcement is due from June 2026.

Definition: Whether the country has enacted comprehensive data protection and privacy legislation. A foundational legal requirement for building trust in digital public infrastructure and for enabling secure cross-border data flows under frameworks like the AU Convention on Cyber Security and Personal Data Protection.
Value Name: Legislation enacted but no enforcement authority
Comments: Comprehensive data protection law enacted (Law No. 2024/017, 23 Dec 2024) but supervisory authority to be created (not yet evidenced as operational).
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Confirmed. Law 2024/017 established the Personal Data Protection Authority (APDP), but legal-compliance sources from early-mid 2026 describe it as 'still being operationalised', with substantive enforcement only due from the June 2026 compliance deadline. As today (6 July 2026) falls just after that deadline, whether APDP is now actively enforcing is unconfirmed in open sources — flagged for human review to check current operational status.

Definition: Whether the country has established policies, regulations, and programmes supporting off-grid and distributed energy solutions (mini-grids, solar home systems). These are critical for extending ICT infrastructure to unserved areas beyond the central grid.
Value Name: Basic policy exists but limited implementation
Comments: Off-grid solar market assessment notes limited policies/regulations and barriers; indicates early-stage off-grid sector with projects underway but constrained policy environment.
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Revised up from a 2019 assessment. ARSEL's 2024 activity report and the Rural Electrification Agency's ongoing rollout across 166 (phase 1) plus 184 (phase 2) localities show active government-led off-grid solar deployment, and CEI Africa (Dec 2025) reports the first-ever private-sector solar mini-grid operating authorisation was just granted to REI Cameroon (Voundou pilot), indicating the regulatory framework now supports private deployment too. This is consistent with 'active policy with some deployment' (code 3) rather than 'limited implementation' (code 2).

Definition: The maturity of the country's technology startup ecosystem, based on the number of tech startups, venture capital activity, accelerators/incubators, and the presence of a supportive ecosystem. Africa's startup scene is well-documented by trackers like Partech, Disrupt Africa, and Briter Bridges.
Comments: Partech-referenced summary indicates funding concentrated in 'big four'; Cameroon not among markets surpassing $50m in equity funding, implying emerging ecosystem with limited funding.
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Revised up. StartupBlink counts 77 startups and 2024 funding of $21.7m (+47.6% YoY), and at least three established hubs (ActivSpaces Douala, Mountain Hub Yaoundé, Silicon Mountain Buea) that have hosted regular events since 2009 (DevFest, CITS, MTN Innovation Challenge). This is more consistent with 'developing... several hubs' (code 3) than 'emerging, 1-2 hubs' (code 2); funding remains well short of the $50m/year threshold for 'established' (code 4).
